title: Clerks passing one folder along
allegory: A solver is like one clerk in a line passing a single folder: each clerk does one small job to its pages, such as adding instructions or wrapping the question in a template, then hands the folder on, and only one clerk carries it to the model and clips in the reply.

cap.1: To test a model you rarely send the bare question. You add instructions, a template, the answer options, a nudge to reason. Everyone used to hand-roll this.
cap.2: Before Inspect, each team kept private eval scripts, so results were hard to compare. The UK AI Safety Institute released Inspect openly in May 2024 as a shared harness.
cap.3: Inspect (UK AISI, 10 May 2024, Open Government Licence) made the eval harness a shared artefact: a dataset, a solver chain and a scorer that someone else can rerun and compare.

cap.1: Picture a line of clerks passing one folder. Each does one small job to the pages, then hands it on. One clerk takes it to the model and clips in the reply.
cap.2: The folder is the TaskState: the chat messages, the user prompt, the model's output and a metadata scratchpad. Each solver edits it and returns it for the next one.
cap.3: A solver is a closure returning async def solve(state, generate), which mutates the TaskState in place and returns it. Metadata persists across the whole chain.

cap.1: A typical line: add a system message, wrap the question in a template, list the options, call the model, then ask for a final choice. A scorer marks it.
cap.2: Inspect ships built-in solvers for jobs like these, so in real work they are library calls. ARENA has you rebuild them, so you know which link to check when a run goes wrong.
cap.3: Order is meaning: solvers before generate() change what the model sees; solvers after it act on the reply. ARENA adds generate() to the list explicitly, never inside a solver.

chapters.name: The template clerk
chapters.title: the folder before and after prompt_template

cap.1: Your exercise clerk does one job: wrap the question in a template, leave every other page alone, and hand the folder on. The reply stays empty until generate.
cap.2: prompt_template(template) returns a solver that rewrites the first user message (state.user_prompt) using the template, then ends with return state.
cap.3: The outer function captures the template; the inner async solve(state, generate) edits the TaskState in place and returns it. It never calls the model: that is generate()'s job.

chapters.name: The silent no-op

right.title: Actually check
lines: every solver ends with return state

chapters.verdict: Before believing the number, read one sample's chat history end to end.

cap.1: The sneakiest bug is a run that works. Place your clerk after the model call: the model never sees your template, nothing complains, the score stays put.
cap.2: An unchanged score after adding a solver is a red flag. Open the log viewer and read one sample: if your template text is not in the chat history, it never took effect.
cap.3: A clean run with an unchanged result is the worst failure signature. The log stores every message, so reading one sample catches it in thirty seconds; the aggregate score never will.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Shape what the model sees, one step at a time
The log shows exactly what was asked

cap.1: Evals are how we find out what a model does. The solver chain decides exactly what it was asked, so it decides what the number means.
cap.2: ARENA's agent loops and AI control exercises are Inspect tasks built from the same parts, and a shared harness lets another team rerun your eval and read the same log.
cap.3: For understanding and steering AI: a result is only as trustworthy as the prompt pipeline behind it. Treat the solver chain as part of the claim, and share it with the score.

caption.1: Match each clerk to its job. Then picture the line in order: which jobs have to happen before the model is called?
caption.2: Everything before generate() shapes what the model sees; anything after it works on the reply. The scorer marks what comes out of the end of the line.
caption.3: The TaskState carries messages, user_prompt, output and metadata through the chain; solvers mutate and return it. Scorers return a Score and can stash metadata of their own.

hamming.what: A small composable step in an Inspect eval that edits the conversation state, such as adding a system message, templating the prompt or calling the model, then passes it on.
hamming.when: Whenever you run an eval with Inspect: the solver chain decides exactly what the model is asked and in what order, before a scorer marks the result.
hamming.why: Splitting the pipeline into small steps makes an eval reproducible and debuggable: swap one step and rerun, and read the log to see exactly what the model saw.

object.title: The folder line
object.subtitle: An Inspect solver chain as a row of stations with one folder threading through every one of them, from the first instruction to the scorer.

cap.1: One folder threads through every station. Each station touches it once and passes it on.
cap.2: The tube is the TaskState: messages, user_prompt, output and metadata, carried through the whole chain.
cap.3: Solvers mutate one shared TaskState in sequence; the chain's order is its semantics.

cap.1: Your exercise station, prompt_template, rewrites only the question page and hands the folder on.
cap.2: It edits the first user message and ends with return state. It does not call the model.
cap.3: A closure over the template string, returning an async solve(state, generate) that mutates and returns the state.

cap.1: The tall station is the only one that talks to the model. Everything to its left shapes what the model sees.
cap.2: Under ARENA's convention no solver calls the model itself; generate() sits in the list explicitly.
cap.3: Making the model call an explicit list entry lets you insert a solver before generation without re-reading any solver's source.

cap.1: From above, the order is plain. Move a template to the right of generate and the model never sees it.
cap.2: A shaper placed after the model call produces a clean run and an unchanged score: the worst kind of bug.
cap.3: Order errors pass every runtime check. Only the log reveals them, because it stores every message the model actually saw.

cap.1: At the end, the scorer marks the answer. Before trusting its number, open one folder and read every page.
cap.2: Use match for multiple choice and model_graded_fact where a string comparison will not do.
cap.3: Scorers return Score objects with optional metadata, and eval() writes a log you can read message by message.

predict.q: You add a prompt_template solver after generate() in the list. What happens to the score?

options.t: Nothing changes: the model never saw the template
It improves, because the template is now in the chain

predict.why: Solvers before generate() shape what the model sees. A template added after the call only rewrites a question that has already been answered.

predict.q: Your new solver changed nothing in the score. What do you check first?

options.t: One sample's full chat history in the log viewer
The average score over more samples

predict.why: The log stores every message. If your template text is not in there, the solver did not run or did not take effect.

predict.q: Under ARENA's convention, which solver calls the model?

options.t: Only generate(), added to the list explicitly
Every solver that edits the prompt

predict.why: No solver calls the model itself, so you can slot a new step in before generation without reading anyone else's code.
